The rain had been falling in a steady, gray drizzle for the past hour, turning the city’s cobblestones into slick mirrors. Anna stood in front of the café’s frosted window, watching the world blur into a watercolor of wet streets and hurried umbrellas. The meeting room smelled of coffee and fresh paint. A half‑stacked pile of flyers lay on the table, and a dozen volunteers shuffled in, clutching notebooks and half‑finished mugs. At the head of the table, Alex, the volunteer coordinator, tapped his pen against a sticky note. “Okay, team,” he said, “we’re here to figure out how to get the fundraiser up and running. We’ve got a budget, a venue, and a deadline. The question is: who will lead the planning committee?” A woman in her thirties, Maya, raised her hand. She’d just joined the group a week ago, and her eyes were bright with enthusiasm. “I think we need someone who can take charge,” she said. “People say that men are naturally better at organizing.

The room fell into a hush, the only sound the faint hiss of the coffee machine in the corner. Maya’s eyes flicked to Alex, waiting for a response. Alex cleared his throat, the pen clacking against the sticky note as he tapped a rhythm that matched the beat of the room’s collective pulse. “Okay, Maya, I hear you,” he said, leaning forward. “But I think the idea that men are the default organizers is a bit… outdated.” He paused, letting the words settle. “We’ve seen teams where a woman has led a project to a successful launch, and teams where a man has struggled to keep everyone on track. Leadership is about skill, not gender.” A murmur rippled through the group. Ben, a volunteer who’d been with the organization for three years, leaned back in his chair, a half‑smile playing on his lips.
